drivingQuestion: In Rabbi Shimon's view, what renders an animal slaughtered without blood emerging susceptible to ritual impurity — the slaughter itself or the blood?
outcomeNote: A mishna lemma plus a single amoraic clarification of it; no question is raised, attacked or answered within this unit.

segments.he: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: הוּכְשְׁרוּ בִּשְׁחִיטָה. אָמַר רַב אַסִּי: אוֹמֵר הָיָה רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, שְׁחִיטָתוֹ מַכְשֶׁרֶת וְלֹא דָּם.
segments.en: § The mishna states (33a): In the case of one who slaughters a domesticated animal, an undomesticated animal, or a bird, and blood did not emerge from them, «Rabbi Shimon says: They were rendered susceptible» to ritual impurity «by means of» the «slaughter» itself. «Rav Asi said» that «Rabbi Shimon would say:» It is «its slaughter» that «renders it susceptible» to ritual impurity, «and not» the «blood» that emerges during the slaughter.

moves.summary: the gemara re-quotes Rabbi Shimon's clause from the mishna at 33a to take it up again
moves.about: re-quoting the mishna's clause that Rabbi Shimon holds the animals were rendered susceptible to impurity by the slaughter itself

moves.cueHe: אמר רב אסי: אומר היה רבי שמעון
moves.summary: Rav Asi delimits Rabbi Shimon's ruling — susceptibility comes from the slaughter, not from the blood
moves.about: what Rabbi Shimon's בשחיטה means — that the act of slaughter alone effects susceptibility to impurity, and not the blood that emerges in it
